stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kahale's argument?
stimulus: Many galaxies eventually stop forming new stars, a change astronomers call quenching. Stars form only when cold gas collapses, so anything that either removes a galaxy's gas or heats that gas can halt star formation. A galaxy's central black hole, when it is actively feeding, can do both: its energetic outflows may blow gas out of the galaxy entirely or merely warm the gas that remains. Astrophysicist Leilani Kahale argues that in dwarf galaxies, active black holes quench star formation chiefly by heating gas rather than by expelling it.
choices: Quenched dwarf galaxies are about three times as likely as star-forming dwarf galaxies of similar mass to have a central black hole that is actively feeding.
Quenched dwarf galaxies with active black holes hold about as much total gas as star-forming dwarf galaxies of similar mass, but far less of that gas is cold.
Quenched massive galaxies with active black holes hold about as much total gas as star-forming massive galaxies of similar mass, but far less of that gas is cold.
Quenched dwarf galaxies with active black holes hold far less total gas than star-forming dwarf galaxies of similar mass, and almost none of that gas is cold.
explanation: Kahale's claim has three parts: it is about dwarf galaxies, it says active black holes cause the quenching, and it says they do it by heating gas rather than by expelling it. The phrase 'rather than by expelling it' is the key. If the black holes were expelling gas, quenched dwarfs would have less gas overall. If they were heating it, the gas would still be there but would no longer be cold. Choice B describes the second case: the total amount of gas matches that of star-forming dwarfs, but little of it is cold. That fits heating and rules out expulsion, in the right kind of galaxy.

A.why: You noticed that the claim links black holes to quenching, and this choice does make that link more likely. But Kahale's specific point is how the black holes do it, heating rather than expelling. A black hole that blew the gas out would produce exactly the same pattern, so this choice leaves the key part of her claim untouched. It is on topic but off claim.

C.why: You saw that the right evidence is gas that is still present but no longer cold. Then you accepted that evidence from the wrong group. Kahale's claim is limited to dwarf galaxies, and a result about massive galaxies doesn't show what happens in dwarfs. The passage gives no reason to assume the two kinds of galaxy work the same way.

D.why: You looked for quenched dwarfs that lack cold gas, which is part of the picture. But this choice says the total amount of gas is also far lower. That points to gas being blown out of the galaxy, which is the very mechanism Kahale's argument sets aside. This finding would weaken her claim, not support it.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's conclusion?
stimulus: Farmers in semi-arid regions often cover their fields with wheat straw. The straw slows evaporation, keeping more water in the soil for crops. But as soil microbes break the straw down, they absorb nitrogen from the soil, leaving less for the crop. In one field trial, maize grown under straw yielded no more than maize grown on bare soil, even though the straw-covered plots stayed wetter. Agronomist Tomás Ferreira concluded that the straw's moisture benefit was real but was cancelled out by the nitrogen the microbes consumed.
choices: In a second trial in which only the straw-covered plots received extra nitrogen fertilizer, maize under straw yielded more than maize on bare soil.
In a second trial in which both straw-covered and bare plots received extra nitrogen fertilizer, maize under straw and on bare soil yielded about the same.
In a second trial in which both straw-covered and bare plots received extra nitrogen fertilizer, maize under straw yielded more than maize on bare soil.
In a second trial with no added fertilizer, the straw-covered plots again stayed wetter than the bare plots in both the driest and wettest months.
explanation: Ferreira says two things at once. First, the straw really does help through moisture. Second, that help was hidden because the microbes used up nitrogen. If both are true, then removing the nitrogen shortage should reveal the moisture benefit. The test only works if both kinds of plot get the same extra nitrogen, so that straw is the only difference between them. Choice C reports exactly that: with nitrogen added to every plot, maize under straw outyields maize on bare soil.

A.why: You had the right idea: add nitrogen and see whether the straw's benefit appears. But here only the straw plots were fertilized, so they differ from the bare plots in two ways, straw and fertilizer. The extra nitrogen alone could explain the higher yield, so this result says nothing about whether the moisture benefit is real. You read more into the result than the setup allows.

B.why: This is the right experiment, with nitrogen added to both groups, but you missed which way the result had to go. If the yields are still equal once the nitrogen shortage is gone, the straw's moisture gave no yield benefit. That is the opposite of the 'benefit was real' half of Ferreira's conclusion, so this finding would weaken it.

D.why: This choice is on topic and true to the passage, since the straw plots do stay wetter. But it repeats something the passage already established and says nothing about yield or nitrogen. It doesn't show that the extra moisture helps the crop, or that nitrogen loss cancelled that help, and those are the two points Ferreira actually concluded.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's claim?
stimulus: In 2022 the city of Marrow Falls turned one car lane on Halvorsen Avenue into a protected bike lane. Over the following year, weekday car counts on the avenue fell by about 4,000. Some residents said the new lane had persuaded commuters to start cycling. Urban planner Ines Okafor disagrees. She claims that most of the decline reflects drivers moving to nearby routes, not drivers giving up their cars.
choices: Weekday bicycle trips on Halvorsen Avenue rose by about 3,800 after the lane opened, mostly by people who used to drive.
Weekday car counts on Halvorsen Avenue had fallen by a similar amount in the year before the bike lane was installed.
Drivers who still use Halvorsen Avenue reported in a survey that their trips have become noticeably slower since the lane opened.
Weekday car counts on the two streets running parallel to Halvorsen Avenue rose by a combined 3,500 over the same year.
explanation: Okafor's claim has two parts: the cars went somewhere else, and that accounts for most of the drop. If the parallel streets gained 3,500 cars while Halvorsen lost about 4,000, most of the missing traffic shows up on nearby routes. That is exactly what 'moving to nearby routes' predicts.

A.why: You matched the topic and missed the direction. A rise in cycling about as large as the drop in cars, mostly by former drivers, is the residents' explanation, the one Okafor rejects. If this were true, it would weaken her claim.

B.why: This questions whether the lane caused the decline at all. Okafor's claim is about where the drivers went, and a decline that was already happening says nothing about whether they rerouted.

C.why: This is the trap that survives the first insight. Slower trips give drivers a reason to reroute, so it feels like support. But a motive to switch routes doesn't show that anyone actually switched, let alone enough people to cover most of the 4,000-car drop.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Reyes's hypothesis?
stimulus: Under a 'live high, train low' program, endurance athletes sleep at high altitude but train near sea level. They often race faster afterward. The thin air at altitude is known to trigger the production of extra red blood cells, which carry oxygen to muscles. Physiologist Tomas Reyes hypothesizes that the faster times come from this rise in red blood cells, not from the confidence athletes gain from an intensive training camp.
choices: Athletes who slept at altitude had higher red blood cell counts at the end of the program than they had at the start.
Elite endurance athletes generally have higher red blood cell counts than recreational endurance athletes have.
Among athletes in the program, those whose red blood cell counts rose the most also improved their race times the most.
Athletes in the program reported feeling more confident before races than they had felt before the camp began.
explanation: The hypothesis is a chain: altitude raises red blood cell counts, and that rise produces faster times. The passage already gives the first link. What needs support is the second link, from red blood cells to race times. If the athletes with the biggest gains in red blood cells also had the biggest gains in speed, the improvement follows the red blood cells and not the camp, which every athlete attended.

A.why: You saw that red blood cells were the key term and stopped there. This confirms only the link the passage already states, from altitude to red blood cells. It says nothing about whether those cells made anyone faster, and that is the link Reyes is hypothesizing.

B.why: This is a general fact about athletes, not about the program. A difference between elite and recreational athletes can't show what caused the improvement in these athletes.

D.why: A boost in confidence is the rival explanation Reyes rules out. Evidence that athletes gained confidence makes that rival more believable, so it works against his hypothesis.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's claim?
stimulus: Excavations at Tell Varin, a Bronze Age farming village, have produced thousands of pottery fragments. Many vessels look like wares from the coastal city of Ashkel, about 90 kilometers away, and scholars have long assumed that the village got most of its pottery by trading with Ashkel. Archaeologist Mira Haddad contends that Varin's cooking pots, whatever their style, were made in the village itself.
choices: The clay in Varin's cooking pots matches a riverbank deposit beside the village and no deposit near Ashkel.
Varin's cooking pots share their shape and rim design with cooking pots excavated at Ashkel.
The clay in Varin's painted serving bowls matches a deposit found only in the hills near Ashkel.
A kiln full of broken cooking pots has been found at a village 30 kilometers from Varin.
explanation: Haddad's claim has two limits: it covers cooking pots only, and it places their production in 'the village itself.' Clay that matches a deposit right beside Varin and nothing near Ashkel ties those pots to the village's own ground and rules out Ashkel as the source.

B.why: Haddad says 'whatever their style,' so she has already set appearance aside. Pots that look like Ashkel's fit the scholars' trade view better than hers. This choice either says nothing about her claim or works against it.

C.why: This is about the right site and the right kind of evidence, but the wrong vessels. Haddad makes no claim about serving bowls, so their source neither supports nor weakens what she says about cooking pots.

D.why: You noticed that local production matters but skipped the scope words 'the village itself.' A kiln at a different village 30 kilometers away shows cooking pots were made somewhere nearby, not in Varin.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Natarajan's hypothesis?
stimulus: A coating developed for car paint closes fine scratches within a day at room temperature. Two features could explain this. The coating holds microcapsules of liquid resin that burst when scratched and seep into the gap, and its polymer chains can slowly flow across a scratch on their own. Materials scientist Priya Natarajan hypothesizes that the flowing chains do most of the repair and that the resin plays at most a minor role.
choices: Samples made without microcapsules closed scratches, but only about half as completely as standard samples did.
Samples made without microcapsules closed scratches almost as completely as standard samples did.
Standard samples closed shallow scratches and deep scratches equally completely within a day.
Polymer chains that flow at room temperature are also found in several other self-healing coatings.
explanation: Work out the direction first. If the resin plays at most a minor role, then removing the microcapsules should barely change how well scratches close. Samples that heal almost as completely without capsules show the chains doing nearly all the work, which is what Natarajan predicts.

A.why: This is the second-order trap. Seeing that the chains heal scratches on their own feels like support, but read the size of the effect. If removing the resin cuts healing in half, the resin is doing about half the repair. That is not a minor role, so this weakens the hypothesis.

C.why: This is an accurate-sounding fact about how well the coating heals. It does nothing to separate the chains' contribution from the resin's, and that split is the whole hypothesis.

D.why: Finding similar chains in other coatings says nothing about how much they do in this coating compared with the resin.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt's conclusion?
stimulus: Paleobotanists often estimate past temperatures from fossil leaves, because woody plants in cool climates tend to have toothed leaf edges and those in warm climates tend to have smooth ones. Plants growing along streambanks, however, often have toothed leaves regardless of climate. In a two-million-year sequence of lake sediments, the share of toothed leaves falls steadily from the lower layers to the upper ones. Paleobotanist Lena Brandt concludes that this pattern reflects regional warming rather than a loss of streamside habitat around the lake.
choices: Smooth-edged leaves in the upper layers are larger, on average, than smooth-edged leaves in the lower layers.
Sediments in the upper layers show that the lake's feeding streams gradually dried up over the period.
Modern woody plants in cool regions around the world more often have toothed leaves than smooth ones.
Pollen in the same layers shows that streamside tree species were about as common at the top as at the bottom.
explanation: Brandt's conclusion has two halves: warming caused the pattern, and loss of streamside habitat did not. The passage itself raises the streambank problem. If streamside trees were just as common in the upper layers as in the lower ones, the habitat explanation fails, and the drop in toothed leaves points to climate.

A.why: Leaf size is a different trait from leaf edges. This is a true-sounding detail about the same fossils that leaves the conclusion untouched.

B.why: Streams drying up means streamside habitat shrinking, which is the explanation Brandt rejects. This would weaken her conclusion.

C.why: This just repeats the general principle the passage starts from. Brandt's conclusion is about why this particular sequence changed, and the principle can't tell warming apart from habitat loss.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moana's hypothesis?
stimulus: At dusk, many wrasses bury themselves in sand and stay there until morning. Burial is thought to offer two kinds of protection: it hides the fish from night-hunting moray eels, and it may block gnathiid isopods, tiny blood-feeding parasites that are active at night. Marine biologist Kai Moana hypothesizes that, at least on reefs where both threats are common, avoiding isopods is the more important benefit of burial.
choices: On reefs that have no moray eels, wrasses kept from burying themselves received far more isopod bites than buried wrasses did.
On reefs with both threats, wrasses kept from burying themselves received far more isopod bites but no more eel attacks than buried wrasses did.
On reefs with both threats, wrasses kept from burying themselves suffered far more eel attacks but no more isopod bites than buried wrasses did.
On reefs with both threats, gnathiid isopods also feed on many fish species that never bury themselves in sand at night.
explanation: The hypothesis compares two benefits and limits itself to reefs where both threats are common. To support it, a finding has to come from those reefs and show burial preventing more isopod harm than eel harm. A big rise in isopod bites with no rise in eel attacks does exactly that.

A.why: This survives the first insight: you saw that isopods matter and found a result where burial blocks them. But it comes from reefs without eels, outside the claim's scope, and with no eels present it can't show isopods are the more important threat.

C.why: This is the right kind of comparison in the wrong direction. Here burial protects against eels and not isopods, the opposite of what Moana predicts.

D.why: This is on topic and about the right parasite, but what isopods eat says nothing about how much burial protects wrasses from them compared with eels.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ashby's claim?
stimulus: Before the 1770s, English weavers making 'cottons' usually ran lengthwise threads of linen through their looms, because hand-spun cotton was too weak to bear the loom's tension. Machine spinning then began producing cotton thread strong enough for that job. Historian Ruth Ashby claims that weavers in the town of Holcombe switched to all-cotton cloth because of this new thread, not because their customers' preferences had changed.
choices: Holcombe weavers kept using linen lengthwise threads until machine-spun thread arrived, though all-cotton cloth had long sold for more.
Holcombe's customers began asking for lighter, all-cotton cloth in the same decade that the town's weavers switched to it.
Holcombe weavers produced noticeably more cloth per week after the switch to all-cotton than they had produced before it.
Machine-spun cotton thread became widely available to weavers across much of England during the 1770s and 1780s.
explanation: Ashby makes two points at once: the new thread caused the switch, and changing customer taste did not. If all-cotton cloth had long sold for more, buyers already wanted it, so demand was not what changed. If weavers switched only when strong thread arrived, the switch lines up with the thread. One finding covers both halves.

B.why: A new customer demand arriving just as weavers switched is the rival explanation Ashby rules out. This would weaken her claim.

C.why: This describes a result of the switch, not its cause. More output after the change says nothing about why Holcombe's weavers made it.

D.why: This supports a broader idea, that the thread spread across England, but says nothing about Holcombe or why its weavers switched. The thread being available nearby doesn't separate Ashby's cause from changing taste.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sol's claim?
stimulus: Agnes Lindqvist's Second Symphony survives in two versions: the 1904 original and a 1907 revision in which the slow movement is shortened and several long-held brass chords are cut. Critics had complained in 1905 that the movement dragged. Musicologist Henrik Sol argues that the brass cuts, at least, were made to suit the echoing acoustics of Stockholm's new concert hall, where the revised symphony premiered in 1907.
choices: Lindqvist's letters from 1905 show that she agreed with the critics that the slow movement was too long.
Lindqvist marked the brass chords for cutting in a draft dated 1905, two years before the Stockholm hall opened.
When the symphony was played in 1909 in a hall with little echo, Lindqvist restored the brass chords but kept the shorter slow movement.
Several composers of the period are known to have revised their works to suit the acoustics of particular halls.
explanation: Sol's claim is narrowed by 'at least': it covers only the brass cuts and ties them to one hall's echo. If Lindqvist put the chords back as soon as she was playing in a dry hall but kept the shortening the critics wanted, then the brass cuts depended on the acoustics and the other change did not. That separates the two revisions the way Sol does.

A.why: This is true to the passage's story but explains the wrong revision. Agreeing that the movement was too long accounts for the shortening, which Sol's 'at least' sets aside. It says nothing about the brass chords.

B.why: This sounds like documentary support, but check the dates. If the cuts were planned before the hall opened, they couldn't have been made for its acoustics. This weakens Sol's claim.

D.why: This is a broader pattern among other composers. That others revised for acoustics makes Sol's idea plausible in general, but it gives no evidence about why Lindqvist cut these chords.
